items.body:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says they are “fairly close” to agreeing on a trade deal with Canada.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday morning, Greer said representatives have “made a lot of progress.”

“I think we’re fairly close on finding a landing zone,” he said.

He noted that Canada’s pursuit of a trade relationship with China “gives some concern and some worry.”

“I think that’s bipartisan,” he said.

Canada and China signed a new trade agreement on Tuesday, which included tariff concessions on Canadian pork and seafood exports as well as relief on Chinese steel and aluminium products.

Greer described the deal as going “a little bit backwards.”

“We’re more inclined to fixing the challenges of globalization,” he said. “(Canada) is more interested in doubling down on globalization.”

He reiterated the desire for a “constructive economic relationship” with Canada, emphasizing that most goods that travel across the border remain duty free and support jobs on either side.

“We’re trying to square the circle between their economy and ours because we are close, we are integrated,” he said. “But there are things like this where we want to make sure we’re protecting the North American economy while also landing on a deal that’s good for the U.S. and good for Canada.”

In response to nearly two years of sporadic trade tensions with the Trump administration, Prime Minister Carney has repeatedly emphasized the importance of diversifying Canada’s trade partnerships beyond the U.S.

Talks on a trade deal had broken down at the 11th hour in August, after which U.S. President Donald Trump had enacted 50 per cent tariffs on most Canadian goods and services. Carney responded with dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs in September, after which followed weeks of trade war escalation on both sides.

In recent weeks, Canadians and U.S. representatives have confirmed that they are back at the table, with both sides hinting at a possible deal in the near future.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada Is Borrowing $765B. Here’s The Problem We Explained To Parliament

This week, we were summoned to Parliament to present evidence to its finance committee. In our opening statement, we chose to focus on explaining the impact of the scale of borrowing on credit markets and the country’s financial stability. The scale of borrowing requires a significant amount of capital to flow into bonds, pushing the cost of borrowing higher for all borrowers. At the same time, the record investment pouring into those bonds is creating a systemic risk the Bank of Canada has quietly referred to as a “self-reinforcing liquidity spiral.”

An MP Asked What Ottawa’s Borrowing Costs Canadians. Here’s the Math

How much will the Government of Canada’s epic borrowing spree cost Canadians? We crunched the numbers in response to Canada’s finance committee’s questions, and estimate it would push the 5-year bond yield 13 to 26 basis points higher. This would cost households up to $8.7 billion in extra interest on their personal loans, but it doesn’t end there. Businesses, and ironically the government of Canada, would also incur higher borrowing costs due to “crowding out.”

Canadian Real Estate Prices Not Expected To Rise Through 2030: BMO

Canadian home prices have fallen 22.8% from peak, and it’s even sharper after adjusting for inflation. BMO Capital Markets warned that real (inflation-adjusted) home prices have made an even steeper drop, the largest since the 1980s. Elevated mortgage rates and weak wage growth are expected to drag prices in real terms through 2030, warns the bank.

Canadian Home Prices Down 23%, Only Reversing 13 Months of Gains

The price of a typical home across Canada slipped 0.3% (-$2.1k) to $649.9k in October. That’s 22.8% below the March 2022 peak, reversing only 13 months of gains. Weak sales and strong inventory suggest the potential for further price declines, but prices still remain out of reach, nearly 4 years after the correction began. The progress—or lack of—emphasizes the scale of exuberance prior to the rate hike shock.

Canadian Inflation Holds At 3.1%, Property Taxes Soar As Arrears Rise

Canadian headline inflation held steady at 3.1% in October, helped by a 2.5% drop in gas prices, though gas prices are still 30.9% higher than last year. October’s CPI also included the annual update for property tax and special charge inflation, which advanced 3.8% year-over-year. While that’s lower than last year, it’s still much higher than the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% average, and comes as property tax arrears in regions like Ontario have surged.

items.title: Chinese investment in Canada’s auto sector to evolve over next year: federal government
items.description: The parliamentary secretary to Prime Minister Mark Carney says China’s investment in Canada’s auto industry will evolve in the next year.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Chinese Lotus EV is pictured. (Annie Bergeron-Oliver/CTV News)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The parliamentary secretary to Prime Minister Mark Carney says China’s investment in Canada’s auto industry will evolve in the next year.
items.body:
The parliamentary secretary to Prime Minister Mark Carney says China’s investment in Canada’s auto industry will evolve in the next year.

“We can both do what we can to protect our existing original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) that are here in Canada — whether that is the (Detroit Three: Ford, General Motors and Stellantis), whether that’s Honda or Toyota — but we also believe there’s a pathway to more industrial investment from the Chinese OEMs,” Kody Blois told CTV Question Period host Vassy Kapelos in an interview airing Sunday.

“I think that’s going to play out over the next year,” he added.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Carney was in China this week and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

While the bilateral led to a new trade deal involving tariffs on pork, seafood, and steel and aluminum products, there has been no update on electric vehicles (EVs) since Carney and Xi’s agreement from January.

At the time, Carney announced a deal that would see Canada reduce its tariff rate from 100 per cent to 6.1 per cent on Chinese EVs and allow up to 49,000 Chinese-made EVs into the Canadian market per year. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on key agricultural and seafood exports, most notably slashing the levies on Canadian canola seed.

Speaking to reporters in Cambodia ahead of APEC this week, Carney signalled he would consider Chinese investment in Canada’s automaking sector if U.S. tariffs continue to disrupt the North American market.

When pressed by Kapelos on the U.S. administration’s staunch opposition to Chinese EVs entering the U.S. market, Blois said that independently of that stance, he believes there’s “a pathway here for investment.”

“Those conversations obviously have to continue,” said Blois, who was also in China with Carney this week. “We have to actually see the proof point of the Chinese EV sales in Canada.”

“And as (Industry) Minister (Melanie) Joly has made clear, our frame will be a joint venture,” he added. “We want to see Canadian equity, we want to see Canadian partnership, and we believe that’s possible.”

Following the sale of Stellantis’ auto assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., to defence manufacturer Roshel, meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford urged the federal government to ensure Chinese-made EV kits are not assembled at the plant.

A Chinese EV kit is essentially an electric vehicle manufactured largely in China, then shipped to another country — such as Canada — in pieces to be assembled into a finished car.

Blois, however, said the government’s focus is not just on kits, but rather on manufacturing and assembly.

“We believe that pathway can happen,” he said. “It’s early days. There’s only been about 17,000 vehicles actually brought into the country this past so far in this, what I would call calendar year, of the quota allocation.”

Blois on preventing foreign interference by China

With a deepening bilateral relationship between the two countries raising public safety concerns among some experts, Blois in his interview also discussed the government’s plan to prevent Chinese interference in Canadian affairs, insisting there are tools to counter meddling.

“At the end of the day, the work the prime minister is doing is really predicated on the fact that we had to get back to some level of engagement, and there were questions certainly about, before the prime minister’s trip, how we engage in that,” Blois said, when asked by Kapelos why the Canada-China relationship reset has not led to a decrease in foreign interference.

A 2025 report from Justice Marie-José Hogue, commissioned by the public inquiry into foreign interference, concluded that China was the “most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institutions.”

“What I would say to the Canadian people is that if you don’t have a leaders-to-leaders meeting, then you don’t even get to the ability to get at the table with Chinese officials to have those really candid conversations,” Blois also said.

He added his government’s position is there are areas for increased partnership with China, including on clean energy and agriculture, while there are other areas that require “guardrails,” namely defence, critical minerals, and artificial intelligence.

When pressed by Kapelos on why engagement with China has not led to better outcomes on national security, Blois said it’s important to have a seat at the table to raise those concerns in the first place.

“We certainly have our own national security profile,” he said. “We have the ability to combat what you’re just raising, the idea of these cyber securities, that’s why we’re making the investments in defence.”

Blois also insisted Canada has both the “mechanisms” and the “institutional power” to counter foreign interference.

You can watch Kody Blois’ full interview on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

items.title: Early test results for U.S. drug ‘one of the biggest breakthroughs’ for cancer, says Canadian oncologist
items.description: An experimental U.S. drug that saw positive results in patients during early tests is a major ‘breakthrough’ for cancer patients, Canadian doctors say.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A doctor tends to patients in his office in Illinois on Oct. 30, 2012. (Jeff Roberson / AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Roberson</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: An experimental U.S. drug that saw positive results in patients during early tests is a major ‘breakthrough’ for cancer patients, Canadian doctors say.
items.body:
An experimental U.S. drug that saw positive results in patients during early tests is a major “breakthrough” for cancer patients, Canadian doctors say.

A U.S. drugmaker reported Friday that its pill, ERAS-0015, reduced tumours in nearly half of the patients with advanced pancreatic and lung cancers in an early-stage clinical trial.

Erasca, based in San Diego, Calif., said 44 per cent of 25 patients with pancreatic cancer saw tumours shrink substantially after they took a 32 mg daily dose of the drug.

Additionally, 69 per cent of patients with the two most common genetic variations of pancreatic cancer experienced positive results after taking the drug.

For lung cancer, tumours diminished in three of five patients (60 per cent) who had previously received immunotherapy and chemotherapy.

Erasca said it would begin late-stage clinical trials to test the drug and another experimental treatment called ERAS-4001 in 2027.

Dr. Jennifer Knox, staff medical oncologist at the University Health Network’s Princess Margaret Cancer Centre in Toronto, will be supervising patients when the clinical trial of the new drug comes to Canada next year as part of the global tests.

“It’s the biggest breakthrough for pancreas cancer probably ever,” Knox said in a phone interview with CTVNews.ca on Friday. “It’s one of the biggest breakthroughs for cancer in general in recent years.”

However, the early stage of the Erasca trial only involved a small number of patients, which Knox said is “typical” at that phase. She expects a large number of people to participate in the upcoming clinical trial in Canada, she added.

‘Big breakthrough’ with another drug

Knox said the first “big breakthrough” targeting the mutant RAS protein that’s present in around 95 per cent of pancreatic cancers actually occurred earlier this year. She said the RAS protein is crucial in the cell metabolism of human beings and can cause cancer when it’s mutated.

The experimental medication “daraxonrasib” had doubled the survival time of patients in a clinical trial, according to a U.S.-led study published in The New England Journal of Medicine in May. The treatment was from another manufacturer called Revolution Medicines.

“It’s been an area of study for like 40 years, and it was thought that they’d never be able to find a drug,” Knox said. “And now there’s like 90 drugs in development that can target this type of mutant protein.”

Knox said Erasca’s drug is similar to daraxonrasib, which is now licensed in the U.S.

“It looks incredibly promising ... So, it’s very exciting,” she said.

Although Erasca CEO Dr. Jonathan Lim said in a press release that the new treatment was “generally well tolerated,” the company had previously reported that one patient taking a 24 mg dose of the drug had died from lung inflammation.

‘A big science win’

In an interview with CTV Your Morning on Friday, Dr. Sam Godfrey with Cancer Research UK said he was optimistic about the pill. He said those receiving treatment for pancreatic cancer normally have less than a year to live.

“Now, that doesn’t mean that cancer’s completely gone… because sometimes microscopic cells remain and they come back, and that’s why we need longer trials,” he said. “But the fact that we’re able to do this and we’re able to target something that previously was never targetable, that is a big science win.”

How does the drug work?

Doctors say pancreatic and lung cancers are typically difficult to treat.

RAS proteins are like “on-off” switches for cell growth and can be harmful if they remain in the “on” mode when they mutate. The new experimental pill ERAS-0015 appears to prevent cancers from developing by blocking mutant RAS proteins that otherwise could allow cancer cells to multiply.

With files from Reuters

items.title: Can a drone really replace a million-dollar farm sprayer in Canada?
items.description: Potato farmers, blueberry growers and researchers gathered at a meeting this week to learn whether drones could make their work easier, as Ottawa expands their use for crop spraying.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A farmer prepares to pilot a drone used to spray pesticides on crops. (Image credit: Chad Mooney)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Potato farmers, blueberry growers and researchers gathered at a meeting this week to learn whether drones could make their work easier, as Ottawa expands their use for crop spraying.
items.body:
ST. PETERS BAY, P.E.I. – Potato farmers, blueberry growers and researchers gathered at a meeting this week to learn whether drones could make their work easier, as Ottawa expands their use for crop spraying.

Under a new federal policy introduced this summer, pesticides already approved for spraying by planes and helicopters can now be applied by drones, too. Previously, those products needed specific authorization for drone use, a barrier because relatively few had received approval.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

In P.E.I., where conventional aerial pesticide spraying remains prohibited, eligible drones offer another way to treat crops from above.

“Anywhere we can kind of save money and increase yield, we’ll usually take a risk on something like that as farmers,” said Chad Mooney, a potato farmer and the founder of AgronomAI, a company specializing in agricultural drone technology.

The equipment could be helpful when fields are too wet for heavy machinery. Drones can also spray tall or delicate crops without risking damage from wheels and reach harder-to-access areas or rough terrain.

Perhaps the biggest benefit is the ability to target specific parts of a field rather than spraying the whole thing.

“That’s cost savings to the producer. And it’s less pesticide use, which is good for the environment,” said Ryan Barrett, research and agronomy specialist with the P.E.I. Potato Board.

In late July, Barrett and other researchers ran a trial comparing a conventional ground sprayer with a drone applying insecticide against Colorado potato beetles in a field in Huntley, P.E.I.

Both treatments proved effective. Six days later, beetle populations had dropped by 100 per cent in the area treated by the ground sprayer and 96 per cent where the drone was used. Neither area needed another insecticide application for the rest of the growing season.

The findings suggest farmers could significantly reduce pesticide use and costs by treating isolated problem areas. Colorado potato beetles tend to start at the edges of fields before moving inward, so farmers could first spray the circumference.

For example, researchers calculated that if a 500-acre potato farm needed to treat just 75 acres, it could save $12,750 in insecticide costs, assuming a product cost of $30 per acre. That doesn’t include potential savings on labour and fuel.

But the technology comes with its own costs and limitations.

A drone can cost between $20,000 and $50,000, according to Mooney, with another $20,000 to $40,000 needed for supporting equipment. That brings the total investment to less than$100,000.

While that might sound steep, it’s far less expensive than a new wheeled sprayer, with a price tag of around $1 million.

“When it comes to cost-benefit analysis and ROI, it’s there if the tool can start to replace this,” Mooney said.

Barrett says drones could also make more sense for farmers who don’t need to spray very often. A corn grower, for example, might only need to spray once or twice a year, making it difficult to justify buying an expensive conventional sprayer.

But a ground sprayer could be more efficient on a very large field that needs to be treated in full. There are regulatory hurdles, too. Some products, including certain herbicides, have yet to be approved for drone use.

Mooney sees another reason to embrace drones: getting younger generations interested in agriculture.

“The drones, an exciting thing for young people that want to farm and learn,” he said.

items.description: Responding to a report that U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a classified memo imposing new restrictions on his country’s military co-operation with Canada, Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said he is in the dark about its contents.

items._ogDesc: Responding to a report that U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a classified memo imposing new restrictions on his country’s military co-operation with Canada, Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said he is in the dark about its contents.
items.body:
HALIFAX -- Responding to a report that U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a classified memo imposing new restrictions on his country’s military co-operation with Canada, Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said he is in the dark about its contents.

“There is some sort of document we haven’t seen,” said McGuinty, while speaking at the Halifax International Security Forum Saturday. He added, when it comes to Canada’s military relationship with the U.S. Armed Forces, it is still business as usual.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

“I can assure Canadians, and I can assure anybody who’s interested, that the Canadian and American co-operation on defence, security and intelligence continues,” said McGuinty.

A bipartisan group of U.S. senators attending the security forum said they had not seen the alleged memo. Several also lamented the tone of the report and suggested it does not help repair or strengthen relations between the two countries.

“The United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada,” said Democratic Delaware Sen. Chris Coons. “It is our hope that on behalf of at least the Congress, to set a consistent positive tone, to express our gratitude for the depth and duration of our relationship.”

Republican South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds minimized the memo’s significance, insisting it would not affect American military personnel deployed in Canada.

“It also does not impact Norad,” said Rounds when describing the joint U.S.-Canadian defence command responsible for monitoring and defending airspace over North America. “It does not impact NATO operations, and it does not impact general or flag officer meetings.”

According to Democratic Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine, when his party takes majority control of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives in 2027, the work to repair the strained relationship with Canada will begin.

“The tone is bad and it is unnecessary. I do think the new congress is going to change the tone dramatically,” said Kaine. “And we are going to do that with a lot of Republican support.”

Dalhousie University international relations professor Robert Huish said that the working partnership between both country’s militaries is still functional and co-operative.

“That needs to be maintained, even if there is political traffic above it,” said Huish. “That is something that military leadership is pretty resilient to.”

McGuinty also announced Canada is joining 24 other allies in the NATO Innovation Fund, which is a multi-sovereign venture capital fund.

“Canada will contribute more than $100 million, opening new opportunities for investment in Canadian startups and innovation funds,” said McGuinty. “For Canadian innovators, that means new investment, new partnerships, and access to international markets.”

Canada is the first country in North America to join the NATO Innovation Fund, which was launched in 2022.

items.title: Paolo Bulgari, the Italian jeweller who turned a family business into global luxury brand, dies at 89
items.description: Paolo Bulgari, the grandson of a Greek silversmith who helped transform the family jewelry business into a global luxury brand synonymous with Italian glamour and design, has died. He was 89.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Paolo Bulgari leaves his residence in Rome, April 14, 1975. (AP Photo/Claudio Luffoli)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Claudio Luffoli</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Paolo Bulgari, the grandson of a Greek silversmith who helped transform the family jewelry business into a global luxury brand synonymous with Italian glamour and design, has died. He was 89.
items.body:
ATHENS, Greece — Paolo Bulgari, the grandson of a Greek silversmith who helped transform the family jewelry business into a global luxury brand synonymous with Italian glamour and design, has died. He was 89.

His family announced his death Saturday, describing him as “the greatest jeweller of our time” and praising his humanity and entrepreneurial talent.

Bulgari presided for decades over a brand celebrated by supermodels, Hollywood stars and collectors for its bold designs and distinctive use of colour.

Born in Rome in 1937, he was the grandson of Sotirios Voulgaris, who founded the jewelry business after leaving Greece. Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewelry, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome, adapting both his craft and his family name to his new home.

Paolo Bulgari joined the family business shortly after leaving school. Working alongside his father, Giorgio, he initially focused on precious stones, developing an expertise in gemstones that would inform his work as a designer and businessman throughout his career.

Turning away from the delicate aesthetic associated with Parisian jewelry houses, the Bulgari family embraced bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected combinations of colour. Drawing inspiration from ancient Rome and Italy’s artistic heritage, the distinctive style helped set the brand apart internationally.

Alongside his brother Nicola and nephew Francesco Trapani, Bulgari led the company’s expansion into major luxury markets, opening stores in New York, Paris, Geneva and Monte Carlo. The business diversified beyond jewelry into watches, perfumes, leather goods and, eventually, hotels.

Heading the group since the mid-1980s, Bulgari guided the company through a period of significant international growth. Its jewelry was a fixture on celebrities spanning from Elizabeth Taylor to Zendaya. Tall and silver-haired, he occasionally appeared alongside the stars wearing his creations, maintaining a characteristically reserved presence.

In 2011, the family sold a controlling stake in the company to French luxury conglomerate LVMH in a deal valued at more than US$5 billion, ending decades of direct family control.

Despite his association with the glamorous world of international luxury, Bulgari frequently referred to his family’s humble start. In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighborhoods on the outskirts of Rome.

“Many people don’t know it,” he wrote in the foundation’s introduction, “but at the origin of my surname there is a story of migration.”

His funeral will be held Monday at the Basilica of Santa Croce in Rome.

Derek Gatopoulos, The Associated Press

items.title: Nations agree to extend talks on AI killer robots but no firm commitment to rein them in
items.description: Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as UN-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Efrem Lukatsky</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as UN-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
items.body:
GENEVA — Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as UN-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the weeklong UN conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn’t commit to binding rules sought by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries and activists.

The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts as major military powers jockey for dominance. It also marked the latest failure to set guardrails for AI, at a time when some experts have warned about such systems breaking out of human control and going rogue.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the UN high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year.

Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.

Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounted to “pushing the can down the road for two more years.”

They noted that most countries supported work toward a new treaty.

Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: “States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities.”

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.

“Technology is moving faster than diplomacy,” said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. “Diplomats are very slow.”

A call for speedy work and alternative routes toward a deal

Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, had set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.

The UN’s Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday and “start thinking about how to get as strong as possible instrument to prohibit and regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems.”

The International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted how autonomous weapons can be “unpredictable” — unlike, say, a bullet fired from a gun with a distinct and predictable trajectory.

“For years, the ICRC and many others have urged states to ensure that humans retain control over the use of force and that life-and-death decisions are never handed over to machines,” it said in a statement.

Advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism at this week’s talks largely by Russia, which, like other leading developers of AI weapons, including the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.

Pope Leo XIV and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened.

Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and any deal is likely to be based on the lowest common denominator.

Jamey Keaten, The Associated Press

OTTAWA -- Firaz Khan works in Ottawa but frequently travels to Toronto to visit his family. So, falling gas prices are providing some much-needed relief.

“It’s a better feeling to know that in a month’s time I won’t be spending as much as I used to,” he said. “Because it was over 500 bucks a month to see my family, so it really bit my wallet.”

Over the past three weeks, the average price of regular unleaded gasoline has dropped by about 28 to 31 cents per litre across the country.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Dan McTeague, president of Canadians for Affordable Energy, attributes the decline in part to the U.S. midterm elections and market expectations that a Democrat-controlled Congress will limit the Trump administration’s war in Iran. The conflict initially contributed to a spike in fuel prices.

“The futures market looks at headlines and potential down the road. They don’t necessarily deal with the real physical market that is prompt or spot prices,” McTeague said.

“They look at what the price might be in a month or two at the point of delivery. On that basis alone, we are seeing markets give back a lot of the so-called war premium, the tension that was there that had been building up for the past eight or nine months.”

Gas prices fell by about 10 cents per litre the day after the U.S. midterm election.

Combined with the federal government’s suspension of the excise tax on gasoline and the seasonal switch to cheaper winter-blended fuel, the national average for regular gasoline now sits at 150.1 cents per litre.

That’s just eight cents higher than the average before the U.S. first struck Iran on Feb. 28.

Diesel prices have also fallen, with the national average now sitting at 228.7 cents per litre. That’s a drop of about 34 cents from a month ago.

But the relief may be short-lived.

Diesel prices typically rise during the winter months as refineries balance production of diesel with demand for home heating oil.

“The likelihood of diesel coming down is limited by the reality that probably starting next week, we’re going to see not just here in Canada, but in the northern hemisphere around the world, temperatures starting to sink,” McTeague said.

“And with that, greater demand for furnace oil and for heating oils. So, this is probably about as good as good as it gets for diesel.”

There is better news for Canadians who rely on regular gasoline.

McTeague expects prices to continue falling for at least another week, with another decrease of eight to 10 cents per litre possible by this time next week.

“This, of course, barring any kind of unforeseen geopolitical event,” he said. “If a strike takes place in Iran or in neighbouring nations, you could see prices reverse themselves.”

items.body:
RICHMOND HILL — Staples Canada says hackers accessed customer information in a cyberattack this month.

A Staples spokesperson says its Staples Print website was breached in early November, adding that none of its other websites were affected.

The spokesperson says data that was accessed included contact information, order summaries and encrypted passwords.

They said no financial data was exposed.

The company says it has secured all accounts and launched an investigation as it assesses the scope of the attack.

It says protecting customer privacy and safeguarding their information is a priority and that it’s taking the matter seriously.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 20, 2026.

The post An MP Asked What Ottawa’s Borrowing Costs Canadians. Here’s the Math appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Federal borrowing could add 13 to 26 basis points to 5-year yields, costing mortgage holders $530 to $1,050 a year and governments billions more in interest.
items.body:
How much does Ottawa’s borrowing cost the rest of us, beyond what shows up in the budget? On Thursday, I testified before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance as part of its study on federal spending power. After I explained the implications of federal borrowing for credit markets, MP Michael Guglielmin pressed for an estimate. I didn’t have one, but it’s a good question, so I began modelling it as soon as I left the room. It’s even more than I assumed.

But first, let’s talk about how debt works.

How Government Borrowing Impacts What You Pay To Borrow

Credit is a market and, like any other, is priced on supply, demand, and risk. When there’s more capital than borrowers, rates fall as lenders compete for business. When borrowing outpaces the capital available, rates rise as borrowers compete for it. Riskier borrowers then pay a premium on top.

The lowest-risk borrower is the Government of Canada, which issues the currency. It pays the least, and its yield is the benchmark that everyone else’s borrowing is priced from. Someone like, I don’t know, Ricky from the Trailer Park Boys would pay the most because he fell behind on his vig.

When Ottawa borrows more, it pushes that benchmark up, and everyone pays more as well. Large businesses, small businesses, your car loan, your mortgage—they’re all priced off the same benchmarks. In finance, this is called crowding out.

Now back to the question. How much extra does this transmission cost, beyond the borrowing itself?

Households Could Pay Billions In Extra Mortgage Interest

We estimate the projected rise in federal market debt will add roughly 13 to 26 basis points to Canada’s 5-year bond yield. That means households can pay billions in extra interest per year once fully phased in, which isn’t exactly chump change. However, that’s just households—the burden extends to businesses and, ironically, the government’s own future financing. Here’s a high-level overview.

The most obvious hit would be to residential mortgages—about $3.2B to $6.3B in extra interest, or $190 to $380 per household per year. However, not all households have a mortgage—about 6 million do. That more realistically puts the burden at an average of $530 to $1,050 per year for those with a mortgage, and it would be concentrated among larger and more recent mortgages.

Applying the same transmission to all household credit puts the upper end at $4.3B to $8.7B per year. That averages about $260 to $520 for each of the 16.6 million households. That doesn’t include the growing use of private lenders, who tend to charge wider spreads as risk compensation.

We also estimate it would reduce borrowing power by roughly 1.3% to 2.6%. Interestingly, Bank of Canada (BoC) research on higher rates points to about the same decline in home prices over two years. If applied to the housing stock, that works out to roughly $111B to $222B in lost home equity. However, let’s stick to more direct costs, as modelling equity losses is a much deeper rabbit hole.

The drag on the housing industry is a more complex issue. While Ottawa’s borrowing is designed to stimulate certain aspects of building, it’s likely to hurt market-based outcomes. That doesn’t mean improved affordability either, since a large share is going towards large corporate landlords. Those are the same firms academics warn have outsized market power, raising rents much faster than mom-and-pop landlords. Another MP asked me about supply and affordability, and it deserves its own rundown next week.

Businesses Can Pay More—Unless They Have Ottawa’s Backing

Businesses face the same transmission. On corporate bonds alone, that’s roughly $1.2B to $2.4B per year in added interest. However, the bigger cost will be investments that no longer clear the higher hurdle rate. In my opening statement, I noted that Ottawa isn’t just providing big businesses with low-cost loans; it’s slanting the odds against the small and medium businesses that employ the majority of Canadian workers. This is part of the fallout: firms with Crown financing are shielded from the higher rate with taxpayer-subsidized loans, while everyone else faces higher costs.

The Irony: Ottawa’s Interest Bill Grows Too

One of the more interesting points is that this will also cost taxpayers. As federal debt is refinanced at higher yields, interest costs rise by roughly $3.1B to $6.2B a year once fully repriced. We use the 5-year yield as a proxy, since 10-year yields move more and T-bill rates less. The same transmission across federal, provincial and local debt works out to roughly $4.7B to $9.5B a year, ceteris paribus. That last part is a ten-dollar word for all else equal, and if you catch me using it in public, feel free to give me a firm slap.

There’s also a risk these estimates don’t capture—liquidity. As I noted in my opening statement, a growing share of Government of Canada bonds are absorbed by leveraged hedge funds. If that liquidity disappears, as it did in March 2020, the Bank of Canada has historically stepped in to buy—the same intervention that left it with roughly $10B in accumulated losses by the end of 2025.

Sounds like a banker’s wet dream, doesn’t it?

Our estimates use research from the CBO, Federal Reserve and Dallas Fed, which finds each point of debt-to-GDP adds 2 to 4 basis points to long-term yields. We scaled that to the 5-year yield using Bank of Canada research, then applied it to the rise in federal market debt projected in the government’s own debt and GDP forecasts. The figures are annual costs once fully phased in, using today’s debt balances, and each stands on its own rather than adding to the others. I’ll provide the committee with the full methodology in my brief, along with estimates for the questions that two other MPs raised.

items.description: Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer
items.content: <p>Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639307993355301439.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Jamie Doolittle on BMO’s support for the broker space as the CMAs draw closer
items.body:
With the Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) just around the corner, BMO BrokerEdge is doubling down on its support for the mortgage broker community as a sponsor of the industry-renowned awards ceremony, now entering its landmark 20th year.

Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge, told Canadian Mortgage Professional the bank was putting its weight behind the CMAs – which take place at Rebel Toronto on Wednesday (November 25) – because of its commitment to a flourishing mortgage broker sector as the housing and mortgage markets continue to evolve.

“BMO BrokerEdge is proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards in celebrating the professionals and organizations making an impact across the broker community,” she said. “Recognizing industry excellence and fostering strong partnerships are at the heart of our commitment to supporting a thriving mortgage broker landscape across Canada.”

Excellence Awardees are up for prizes across a range of shortlisted categories at the event, with awards recognizing the leading brokers, lenders, service providers, and more.

Other awards up for grabs include the Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizing an individual who has made an outstanding contribution to the sector over a lengthy career.

Doolittle said honouring the industry’s top performers benefits the wider mortgage space. “Recognizing excellence shines a light on the professionals and organizations driving meaningful progress across the sector,” she said.

“Their commitment to innovation, client service, and collaboration strengthens the broker channel and leads to better outcomes for Canadian homebuyers.”

The CMAs draw nominations from brokers, brokerages, lenders, underwriters, business development managers (BDMs), and service providers from coast to coast.

A significant year for BrokerEdge

With 2026 winding to a close, Doolittle said the year has been an important one for BMO’s mortgage broker relationships. “2026 has been a milestone year for BMO BrokerEdge, marked by our national expansion and ongoing investment in the broker channel,” she said.

“As more Canadians choose to work with mortgage brokers, we remain focused on improving our service, processes, and programs to help brokers meet their clients’ evolving needs.”

Doolittle said a key priority for the company this year has been improving the day-to-day experience for brokers and their clients by enhancing the overall experience and continuing to improve products, processes, and digital capabilities.

She singled out the lender’s rate guarantee as one way BrokerEdge aims to stand out. “We will continue to differentiate our offering with features such as our 130-day rate guarantee, providing greater flexibility and confidence to homebuyers,” she said.

The company has also rolled out process changes through the year. “We’ve implemented process enhancements, helping create a more seamless and efficient experience,” Doolittle said. “This reflects our ongoing commitment to make it easier for brokers to do business with BMO BrokerEdge and deliver strong outcomes for their clients.”

Looking ahead to 2027

In the year ahead, BMO BrokerEdge intends to keep investing in the broker channel – including resources and support to help brokers grow their business and serve their clients, according to Doolittle.

She said the broker community was an essential part of the big steps taken by the company in recent times. “We would like to thank our broker partners across Canada for their continued trust, collaboration, and support throughout the year,” she said.

“The success of our channel is built on strong relationships, a shared commitment to clients, and a collective focus on raising the bar for our industry.”

Nobody has a crystal ball when it comes to what’s in store for 2027, but Doolittle said she’s optimistic about what’s around the corner for the mortgage industry and market. “As we look toward 2027, we’re optimistic about the opportunities ahead and remain committed to investing in the broker channel, investing in our capabilities, and helping our partners deliver exceptional outcomes for Canadian homebuyers,” she said.

items.content: <p>As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307927281564307.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: As the CMAs mark their 20th year, sponsors and brokers say private lending has never mattered more
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) mark their 20th anniversary on November 25 at Rebel Toronto – and the private lending category has never been more hotly contested.

With private mortgage originations in Ontario reaching $32 billion in 2024, up from $11 billion a decade earlier according to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), the Broker of the Year – Private Lending award has become one of the ceremony's most closely watched honours.

For Joe Flor, vice-president of national sales and broker relations at CMI Financial Group in Toronto, which sponsors the award, the recognition carries real industry weight.

Private mortgage lending in Ontario accounted for 15.8% of all mortgage originations in 2024, according to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA)'s annual Private Residential Mortgage Lending Report, released in August 2025.

While that figure represents a slight contraction from prior years, the decade-long trend has moved sharply upward – from $11 billion in privately funded mortgages in Ontario in 2015 to $32 billion in 2024, per FSRA data.

For CMI, which sponsored the Broker of the Year – Private Lending award at the 2026 CMAs, the event is more than a celebration.

"I think it's important for us to recognize lenders and brokers that excel in their profession and in their trade," Flor told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"It sets the standards for all those that are coming into the industry and also for other lenders who are trying to improve their broker experience."

The 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards is proud to partner with Canadian Mortgages Inc. in recognizing excellence with the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending. #MortgageAwardsCA Book a table: https://t.co/hrh5z64Cj6 https://t.co/j3G74SCkSy — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 16, 2026

Knowing the lender matters as much as knowing the product

Flor pointed to a persistent gap he sees in how some brokers approach private files – one that grows more consequential as more Canadians turn to private channels due to qualification challenges, elevated debt-to-income ratios, and credit blemishes that prevent them from accessing traditional lending.

"It's important to understand the specialized solutions available," he said.

"It's also important to understand the lender that you're partnering with because there are a lot of private lenders and it's kind of overwhelming when you're trying to figure out which lender to partner with."

The importance of due diligence on the lender side is not purely a commercial concern.

FSRA's consumer research found that the mortgage delinquency rate among non-bank lenders rose to 0.20 per cent in the third quarter of 2024, up from 0.14 per cent in the same quarter of 2022, according to Statistics Canada. The regulator has identified insufficient exit strategies as one of the key risks for private borrowers, and has maintained private mortgage brokering as a supervisory priority in both its 2024–25 and 2025–26 supervision plans.

For Flor, that underscores a responsibility brokers carry when placing clients in private products.

"Credibility goes a long way," he said.

"You want to know you're putting your client in the right solution with the right lender and not compromising them, potentially in a year or two down the road."

The 2026 excellence awardees for the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending include Cheryl Pienta of FC Funding, David Clarke of TMG The Mortgage Group, Davinder Powar of AKAL Mortgages Inc., and Geoff Lee of GLM Mortgage Group.

CMI Signature and a push toward one-stop-shop lending

Ahead of the ceremony, CMI has been moving on a product expansion it hopes will deepen its value to the broker channel. The lender launched its CMI Signature product in Ontario this week – a new offering aimed at broadening its reach beyond its core private lending mandate.

Flor described a second product launch slated for the following week, which he characterised as an alt-minus solution, alongside several additional products targeted for release in early to mid-2027, subject to third-party approvals.

The broader ambition, he said, is to become a one-stop-shop lender capable of offering a graduation program – a pathway that would allow clients who enter CMI as private borrowers to transition through the lending spectrum into more conventional products as their financial profiles improve.

"CMI is really focused on the broker experience, the customer experience, and providing those solutions and also ensuring that the ease of that transaction is there," he said.

"A lot of digitisation, a lot of technology is being poured into it, and we want to be one of the leaders in the industry of driving that technology aspect of it."

items.title: Finmo's Sidekick: the AI assistant that knows your deals
items.description: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.content: <p>Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_639307939243156766.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.body:
Most brokers have tried AI tools to draft emails and answer quick questions. What they haven't had is an AI assistant that knows their deals and can work on them.

Lendesk built Sidekick to close that gap. Sidekick launched in open beta at Finmo Momentum 2026 on November 24 and it's a new AI assistant inside Finmo, Lendesk's mortgage origination platform. It runs in a chat panel next to the broker's deals, where it reads the application and documents, makes updates on request, and looks up lender rates and guidelines. The broker never has to leave the deal.

“We wanted to give brokers a tool that actually works the deal, instead of just surfacing information about it. Sidekick knows the deal, knows the lenders, and takes on the admin, so brokers can spend more time with clients,” said Carter Zimmerman, president of Lendesk.

From single tasks to the whole deal

Each of Finmo's earlier AI tools did one job. In 2024, Finmo added AI deal create, which builds a new application from an email chain, call transcript or notes, and AI fill from document, which pulls property details from an MLS listing into the deal. This year Finmo added AI down payment verification and income verification, which cut hours of document review down to minutes.

Sidekick works differently. It doesn't run one fixed process. It can help with any task a broker does in Finmo: building and editing deals, managing documents, running down payment and income verification, calculating GDS/TDS, and researching lenders.

“Our first AI tools each solved one problem well. Sidekick ties them together,” Zimmerman said. “For the first time, a broker can ask for help the way they’d ask a colleague and get it across the whole deal.”

Ask Sidekick to organize and review a deal’s documents, and it renames files consistently, moves them into the right document conditions, and adds any missing conditions. It then runs down payment and income verification.

Ask Sidekick which rental income approach works best for a conventional deal, and it compares lenders’ add-back and offset policies using Lender Spotlight. It estimates the impact on GDS/TDS and compares available rates and requirements, helping identify the best fit and the lowest-rate option that meets the lender’s stated qualifying limits.

“Sidekick takes what you thought was a B deal and turns it into an A deal,” said Joe Tomkins, Director of User Development & Enablement at Lendesk.

Placing the deal

Sidekick connects to Lender Spotlight, so it can match a deal against lender policies and pull current rates. The "Place this deal" flow works the deal the way an experienced broker would. It grades the deal, screens lenders on their guidelines, and compares rates. Then it gives one recommendation, with a short list of alternatives.

“Finding the right lender for a deal takes experience, plus a lot of checking rates and guidelines across dozens of lenders,” Zimmerman said. “Sidekick handles the checking in one request, so brokers get to the right shortlist faster.”

The broker makes the call

By default, Sidekick asks before it changes anything. Each update, whether it's an edit to the application or a credit pull, shows up as an approval card with the exact change. Nothing is saved until the broker approves it. Read-only tasks, like reviewing the deal or running GDS/TDS numbers, happen right away.

Sidekick also works within the broker's own permissions, so it can only see and do what that broker already can in Finmo — and brokers can delete their chat history at any time.

“In mortgages, trust isn't optional,” Zimmerman said. “That's why Sidekick shows every change before it's made. The broker is always in control.”

Sidekick is available now in open beta, free while the beta runs. Brokers already on Finmo can ask their team admin to turn it on through Finmo support. Brokers new to Finmo can sign up and request access when they join.

items.title: Most Canadians are planning retirement without their biggest asset
items.description: Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use
items.content: <p>Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307922816363281.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Most Canadians are sitting on a retirement resource they haven’t thought to use
items.body:
Two-thirds of Canadian homeowners rank their property as their single largest financial asset, yet only 27% consider that housing wealth a resource for retirement, according to new research from HomeEquity Bank and Ipsos.

The contrast with registered savings instruments is stark. Sixty-six percent of homeowners rank their property as their primary financial asset. Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) or Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs) come a distant second at 8%, followed by workplace pensions at 6% and Tax-Free Savings Accounts (TFSAs) at 4%.

However, only 27% consider home equity a viable resource in Canadian retirement planning. The home is treated as wealth, not income.

The gap between asset and cash flow

Among survey respondents, 41% feel financially secure but worry about having enough readily available cash, while 40% are not confident they could absorb a major unexpected expense without significantly changing their lifestyle.

Retiring with mortgage debt is fast becoming the norm for Canadians, adding a further layer of pressure. Among those approaching retirement, 35% have delayed their planned retirement date and 49% expect to work part-time.

Among retirees, 29% are spending more monthly than anticipated, with 28% drawing more heavily on investments than planned.

“Canadians have done something incredibly important over their working lives: they’ve built wealth,” said Pattie Lovett-Reid, chief financial commentator at HomeEquity Bank in Toronto, Ontario.

“Retirement planning isn’t just about accumulating assets. It’s about having the right combination of assets, income and cash flow throughout retirement.”

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

A growing opportunity for brokers

Pierre Martin, senior vice president, broker channel at HomeEquity Bank, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in August that the reverse mortgage conversation is increasingly central for brokers working with existing clients.

“Segment your database. Reconnect with clients aged 55 and older. Ask better questions about retirement and family goals, and know when to bring home equity back into the conversation,” he said.

Rene Quercia, also senior vice president, broker channel at HomeEquity Bank, reinforced that message in a February event.

“In many cases, older folks are retiring with mortgages or with debt and interest rates on that debt are going up, not down. So I think many brokers, when they’re faced with these types of clients now, see reverse mortgages as a good option to present to clients,” he said.

Yvonne Ziomecki-Fisher, chief customer, brand and advice officer at HomeEquity Bank, said home equity deserves inclusion in every retirement planning discussion. 

“Home equity won’t be the right choice for everyone, but it deserves a place in the retirement planning conversation. For some homeowners, it can provide greater flexibility, strengthen cash flow and help manage unexpected expenses while allowing them to continue living in the home they love,” she said.

The Ipsos survey was fielded October 26–27, among 1,500 Canadians aged 18 and older.

items.title: Bank of Canada warns against excessive reliance on rate signals
items.description: Deputy governor Toni Gravelle says over-reliance on forward guidance can distort market signals
items.content: <p>Deputy governor Toni Gravelle says over-reliance on forward guidance can distort market signals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639307886080356256.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Deputy governor Toni Gravelle says over-reliance on forward guidance can distort market signals
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is urging financial markets to exercise independent judgment on the rate outlook rather than simply reflect the central bank’s own signals.

Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle, speaking before the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce in Edmonton, Alberta, on November 18, warned that too much forward guidance — public signalling of where the overnight rate may head next — risks eroding the independent analysis markets must apply.

The speech follows the Bank’s decision to raise its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.50% at its October 28 announcement, its first hike in more than three years. The final rate announcement of the year set for December 9.

“In a sense, they stop doing their homework,” Gravelle said. “As a result, central banks can lose an important source of information about how investors view the economy.”

The comments echo warnings issued by Kevin Warsh, the new chair of the United States Federal Reserve, who argued in August that forward guidance risks locking policymakers into future decisions.

When scenarios replace explicit guidance

Rather than committing to a rate path, Gravelle said the Bank of Canada has leaned more heavily on scenario analysis — alternative economic projections that show how monetary policy might react if key risks materialize.

A scenario published in the April Monetary Policy Report (MPR) assumed oil prices, then near US$100 per barrel, would ease to roughly US$75 per barrel by mid-2027.

By October, the actual path had tracked the more adverse outcome.

“In the April high oil price scenario, inflation stays close to 3% for more than a year, and consecutive policy rate increases are needed to get inflation back to target,” Gravelle said. That scenario, he noted, had by October largely materialized.

Canada's annual inflation rate held at 3.1% in October, strengthening expectations that the Bank of Canada may pause at its December 9 rate decision as markets assess easing price pressures and softer economic data. https://t.co/jzZrTP5pgU — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 17, 2026

What higher rates mean for brokers

According to the Bank of Canada’s Q3 Market Participants Survey, financial market participants revised their five-year Government of Canada bond yield} forecasts upward by 35 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.50%, with the consensus terminal policy rate settling at 2.75%.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Canada, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in September that clients should not wait on pre-approvals.

“So it is a time when we should encourage anyone that is interested in potentially buying a home that they get pre-approved, because today’s rates, even though they’re a little above what they were last week and the week before, they’re only going higher,” she said.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, Ontario, said the October rate hike was designed to buy time.

“We think this hike buys the Bank a few months to assess whether higher energy and input costs are actually filtering through to consumer prices,” he said, projecting one further 25-basis-point increase in Q1 2027.

items.title: Montreal fintech nesto names SVP to accelerate operational growth
items.body:
nesto group(e), the Montreal-based mortgage technology and lending platform, has appointed Louis-François Poirier as Senior Vice President, Strategic Operations. The company says the hire will accelerate execution and unlock new opportunities across its fast-growing Canadian lending business.

Poirier reports to Damien Charbonneau, Co-founder and Chief Operating Officer of nesto group(e).

A veteran operator joins a fast-moving platform

Poirier arrives with more than two decades of senior leadership across two of Canada’s most prominent financial institutions.

He spent 17 years at National Bank of Canada in Montreal, advancing from credit risk analyst through mortgage product management, credit card products, and customer strategy.

From 2020 to 2025, he held a succession of vice-presidential roles at Desjardins — culminating as VP of Retail Lending, Everyday Banking and Savings Products — where he led five business lines with direct profit-and-loss accountability and oversaw two major technology transformation programmes: a loan origination system overhaul and a core banking platform migration.

Most recently, he ran LFP Conseil, an advisory firm he established in January, where he partnered with executive teams on portfolio performance, credit strategy, and operating model scalability before joining nesto group(e).

“After 20+ years in financial services, I’m drawn to nesto’s ambition to reshape Canadian lending,” Poirier wrote in a LinkedIn post.

“I can’t wait to roll up my sleeves with the team and scale our business.”

His appointment follows a period of significant momentum. The company closed a C$302-million Series E financing round in June at a C$1.47-billion valuation, now administers more than C$80 billion in mortgages, and reported over C$37 billion in originations through 2026 alone.

In October, Deloitte ranked nesto #9 on its Technology Fast 50 list, recognising 3,311% revenue growth over three years.

Building the lending ecosystem of the future

Founded in 2018 by Malik Yacoubi, Charbonneau, Karim Benabdallah, and Chase Belair, nesto group(e) operates across the nesto, CMLS, and Intellifi brands and licenses its Nesto Cloud platform to partners including IG Wealth Management, Equitable Bank, and Canada Life.

Its June 2024 acquisition of CMLS Group — formerly Canada’s third-largest independent mortgage finance company, with more than 50 years of operating history — extended the platform into commercial origination, asset management, institutional servicing, and software licensing across all Canadian jurisdictions.

The company employs more than 1,000 people nationwide and has been named Canadian Mortgage Lender of the Year by the Canadian Lending Association in both 2023 and 2024.

items.body:
Opening Statement before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance

Stephen Punwasi, Co-Founder and Chief Data Analyst, Better Dwelling.

Ottawa, November 19, 2026.

As prepared for delivery.

Thank you, Madam Chair, and members of the committee.

My name’s Stephen Punwasi, and my background is in behavioural finance and the levers that drive asset prices. I’m also the co-founder of Better Dwelling, Canada’s largest independent housing news outlet, where we focus on reducing information asymmetry.

Information asymmetry occurs when one party is better informed about a transaction than the other. This slants the odds in their favour, helping them to win. Since there’s no shortage of people willing to sing the praises—or fear mongering—over government spending, I’m going to do what we do at Better Dwelling and just explain the market dynamics and risk, hoping it reduces the asymmetry for all parties.

So let’s talk about borrowing, debt, and risks.

There are three things households and policymakers should understand about credit markets.

One: debt is future income, spent today, plus interest.

Borrowing for productive uses can pay for itself. The public is generally in agreement here, and the language Ottawa’s using resonates with that sentiment. However, an investment has to produce a return after its costs, including interest and opportunity costs.

Right now, Ottawa can’t tell us where the money is going. Roughly $260 billion is going to Crown Corporation loans and equity, and the budget doesn’t break down which ones get what. Housing is a good example. The PBO previously said it was unclear if the spending helped or just took credit for things that were happening. Since then, Ottawa ramped up the spending, building costs dropped, and fewer homes are being built. It costs less to build a home, the subsidies have climbed, and fewer are being built. That makes it pretty clear.

The bank grills me if I want to take my own money out for a used car. $260 billion is the equivalent of 16 million Canadian households going to work and paying taxes for a year, but Ottawa won’t tell the public where it’s going?

Two: The Price of Debt Depends On Who’s Borrowing

Debt is priced by supply, demand and risk. Ottawa borrows at the lowest rates in the country, since it runs the printing press. The issue is what happens next. Through its Crown corporations, it passes that cheap credit on to the projects it chooses.

Everyone outside those programs borrows at market rates. Small businesses can’t issue bonds, neither can households. They have to borrow from banks, and according to the latest lending conditions survey, face tighter conditions. Ottawa isn’t just borrowing, it’s helping big businesses succeed, while slanting the odds against the small and medium businesses that employ the majority of Canada’s workers. That’s a subsidy, and like any corporate handout, the public should know what it’s paying for.

Three: Know Your Lender & How Long They’ll Stay

Policymakers have been boasting of the foreign investment made in Canada, but they’ve been light on the details. Let me help with that. Almost zero of the net investment has been in equities. It’s all debt. Foreign investors absorbed all of Ottawa’s net new issuance in the first half of this year. This has created a tail risk that threatens the whole financial system, and I’m not just being hyperbolic. The Bank of Canada has quietly confirmed it.

Hedge funds account for over 40 percent of purchases at auctions, and typically fund those positions with overnight or short-term borrowing. They aren’t lenders the way a household thinks of one. They’re renting the bonds, on borrowed money, a day at a time.

The Bank of Canada warns that a funding disruption could force them to sell suddenly, calling it a “self-reinforcing liquidity spiral.” If I were advising a hedge fund today, I would tell them to make that play too.

During the last crisis, fiscal dominance forced the BoC to buy government bonds to provide liquidity. It was a big payday for investors; the BoC ended up with a $10 billion loss, the equivalent of 625,000 households’ federal taxes for a year.

It will happen again. A crisis for Canadians is a massive win for these foreign investors. Make no mistake, this play is a bet against Canada, not for it. This will be the difference between a recession and a financial crisis.

That backstop keeps Ottawa’s borrowing cheap today. The risk doesn’t go away. It moves to the public.

Is Ottawa making responsible investments for the future of Canada? I don’t know, and anyone who definitively says it is or isn’t is lying. Because Ottawa isn’t sure where the money is going either, it’s like the funds are allocated before anything is actually planned.

I’d ask the committee for three things. First, asset-level reporting for Crown lending and equity, including the subsidy built into below-market loans, so Parliament can see where the spending goes—and the public knows what their kids will be paying for. Second, outcome reporting for conditional transfers like housing. It’s simply not enough to spend money and take credit for wins and blame the economy for the losses. Third, reporting on who holds federal debt, how concentrated that base is, and how much of it is funded with short-term leverage, alongside each budget.

Banks and investors would ask those questions. Parliament—and the public—should be able to ask Ottawa them.

Thank you. I’m happy to take your questions.
